image_description: A close-up, side-view photograph of a male mallard duck (drake) floating on water. The image captures the rear half of the body, highlighting the iridescent blue speculum feathers bordered by white stripes on the wing, the curled black central tail feathers, and the mottled brown/grey flank plumage. The head is partially visible on the far left but mostly out of frame. The water surface shows realistic ripples and reflections.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head and bill are largely outside the frame or obscured by the angle; only the back of the neck/head area is barely visible.
The eye is not visible in this cropped rear-angle shot.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the body shows dense, layered feather texture consistent with waterproof plumage. The buoyancy and interaction with water appear physically correct.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: While the green head is not fully visible, the visible wing pattern (blue speculum with white borders) and the grey/brown mottled flank feathers are characteristic of a male mallard's breeding plumage.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The legs and feet are submerged or hidden beneath the body/water line and are not visible.
The folded wing structure is visible, showing the correct layering of flight feathers and the distinct speculum patch.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The characteristic upward curl of the central black tail feathers is clearly visible and structurally sound.
